newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SAFRICA CELL PHONE TENTACLES SPREAD TO COUNTRYSIDE.
newsitem.headline: SAFRICA CELL PHONE TENTACLES SPREAD TO COUNTRYSIDE.

text.p: South Africa's booming cellular phone industry is spreading its tentacles into rural areas where inadequate existing infrastructure has left people clammering for service, industry officials said on Thursday.
The country's first cellular network for public telephones was launched by Post and Telecommunications Minister Jay Naidoo in the former Transkei homeland in the Eastern Cape on Thursday.
Service providers, Vodacom and MTN, have both rolled out their networks in the Eastern Cape over the last four months, at a total investment of about 50 million rand.
They have completed 20 base stations between them and Vodacom plans four more shortly while three community telephone shops were switched on this week.
Vodacom chairman Alwyn Martin predicted a bright future for mobile phones -- already a standard in cities -- in areas such as the former Transkei.

No network extension or upgrading has taken place in the Transkei since 1988, when the homeland regime was overthrown, and there is a backlog for 30,000 telephones. At present, only 19,000 phones serve a population of four million.

"This huge pent up demand has generated enormous cellular call volumes on Vodacom's network, with our two base stations in Umtata clocking up 10,000 calls per day, making them two of the busiest sites in the country," Martin said.
"Within four months we have expanded Transkei's telecomms infrastructure by 10 percent."

Vodacom, which earlier announced it had signed up its 400,000th subscriber, is 50 percent owned by state-owned Telkom, with 31.5 percent held by the Vodafone Group Plc of the UK and 18.5 percent by the Rembrandt Group Ltd .
Eastern Cape Premier Raymond Mahlaba said that the deliberate neglect of telecommunications during the apartheid era had left installations in a serious state of disrepair.
"To add insult to injury thieves are on a daily basis stealing the copper wire and cables, which could be decribed as a form of political sabotage," he added.
